hypothesis: Among the simplest equational axiom systems for one binary operator (single equations with at most four operator occurrences), the large majority admit several non-isomorphic finite models (operator forms) on 2 and 3 elements, and only a small minority force a single form.
pass_criterion: Pre-registered. Family: all single-equation axiom systems lhs == rhs where lhs and rhs are terms built from one binary operator and variables, with a total of n = 1..4 operator occurrences in the equation, variables named canonically in order of first occurrence (a, b, c, ...) reading lhs then rhs, excluding equations with lhs identical to rhs, and identifying an equation with its side-swapped twin (so each unordered pair of sides is counted once). For each axiom system and each k in {2, 3}, enumerate all k^(k^2) operator tables (16 and 19,683), keep those satisfying the equation for every assignment of the variables, and count the models up to isomorphism (relabelling of the k elements by any permutation): m2 and m3. Definitions: 'many forms' = m3 >= 3; 'single form' = m2 <= 1 and m3 <= 1 and m2 + m3 >= 1; 'no non-trivial form' = m2 = m3 = 0 (only the one-element model). The claim PASSES if the fraction of axiom systems with 'many forms' is >= 0.80 and the fraction with 'single form' is <= 0.05. Reported, not decisive: the same fractions restricted to n = 4; the list of 'single form' systems; the systems whose k = 2 model set is exactly {Nand, Nor} (operators 7 and 1 in Wolfram's numbering) or {Xor, Xnor} (6 and 9); and, as a validation of the model-finding code against the note 'Properties of operators from axioms' (p. 1171), the k = 2 model sets of all lhs == a systems with up to 6 operators under this canonical labelling, listing how many allow only {6, 9} and only {1, 7} (the note reports 32,004 and 964 for its family of 274,499 systems; the family definition in the note is not fully specified, so this is a plausibility check, not a decisive comparison).
fail_criterion: Pre-registered. The claim FAILS if fewer than 50% of the axiom systems have 'many forms', or if more than 20% force a 'single form'. Between those bounds and the pass thresholds the verdict is 'mixed'. If the enumeration cannot be completed for k = 3 within the run-time budget the verdict is inconclusive (underpowered).
interpretation: Wolfram's pictures (pp. 804-805) show, for a sequence of simple axiom systems, the operator forms (multiplication tables) allowed with 2, 3 and 4 elements, inequivalent under relabelling; his claim is that the vast majority of systems allow many forms and are 'not really about operators of any particular form', while a few (logic, i.e. Nand; junctional, equivalential and implicational calculi) force essentially a single form. This test reproduces that model enumeration for k = 2 and 3 only (k = 4 would require 4^16 tables per axiom, beyond the budget) over an explicit, exhaustively enumerated family of the simplest single-equation systems. 'Vast majority' is read as >= 80%, 'only a few' as <= 5%. Multi-axiom systems (e.g. group theory) are outside the enumerated family and are not needed for the majority statement.

datasets.name: All single-equation axiom systems for one binary operator with 1-4 operator occurrences, canonical variable labelling (generated by analysis.py)
datasets.version: generator in analysis.py; Wolfram operator numbering: table digit at position k*x + y (least significant = f(0,0)) as in the note 'Implementation of operators from axioms' p. 1171
datasets.role: axiom family under test; finite models on 2 and 3 elements enumerated exhaustively
